title: Which Kurosawa films have the broadest appeal?

For me Sanjuro is a perfect distillation of all that is good in the films of Kurosawa–it satisfies both as art and entertainment, and at less than a hundred minutes it doesn't overstay its welcome. The introduction of Toshiro Mifune's character is flawless and hooks you right into the narrative. And though the tone is largely comedic, there's an undercurrent of darkness that almost literally erupts in the final scene. If I were going to introduce someone to Kurosawa's work, Sanjuro would be my first choice.

I recommend Rashomon for all Kurosawa newbies. The concept is intriguing. Everyone in a situation has their own experience, and it can be based on everything from reality, faulty memories, or lying. Rashomon causes the viewer to ask what actually happened, which story is real.

His adaptations of Shakespeare's plays are a good starting point: Throne of Blood (1957) and Ran (1985). 

Rashomon (1950) is the most obvious answer I think, and is one of the better choices (especially good to put to a first-timer). After them, I think you can also say that The Bad Sleep Well (1960), The Seven Samurai (1954) or one of his color movies have a broad appeal. 

(Of his color movies, I think the aforementioned Ran, Dreams (1990) and maaaaaybe Dersou Uzala (1975) are good to go).

Yojimbo is fairly tame ultimately but I'd argue there's real novelty in seeing it the first time even today. Even if you don't have the specific context, it really *feels* like an old Samurai movie somebody made after seeing a Western for the first time. Even someone who has never seen a Leone film could watch this and think, *"Ohh, that's where that clever insolent gunslinger figure comes from."*

The best part of High and Low is the consistent reoccurring thought of *"Damn! This is weirdly tense"* as the awkward class distinctions and stilted kidnapping plot layer on top of each other. I think it works best when it's a contrast to the gradual momentum of his historical pieces, which makes it less than ideal for a first exposure. Gnarly though it is.
Some of the performances in Kurosawa films, especially from Mifune, are over the top in a way that can be distracting for viewers used to a more "naturalistic" style

Really surprised nobody is saying *Hidden Fortress* 

It's got very broad appeal, especially for younger people. An adventure film about Samurai and a hidden princess, what's not to like?

Broad acting is a term used to describe acting that involves more exaggerated expressions and delivery of lines. It's not inherently better or worse but tends to be more dramatic than realistic and was more common during the black & white era of films (possibly partly to do with the carryover from theatre to cinema in earlier talking pictures), whereas modern Western cinema tends to regard a more restrained naturalistic style as preferable. You still find broad performances in modern Hollywood, but they are more usually associated with films that have an element of camp built in to them, so realism in a portrayal is less important.

It's a stylistic preference, and if someone watches a lot of anime or Korean dramas, for example, they'll find plenty of broad performances, but if you're not used to it because you're mostly exposed to modern Hollywood, it may feel a bit jarring.

Going by your sentiments on High and Low, OP, and it's one of my absolute favorite of Kurosawa's films, maybe by "broadest appeal" we could talk about his other noir/crime films, as I understand it's not a genre with cultural specifications relative to Japan, like samurai films (even if they served as inspiration for lots of westerns).

*Drunken Angel* and *Stray Dog* may have this "broad appeal" in sense that they are crime/noir films (a genre for which Kurosawa got a lot of Hollywood inspiration), but for the fact they weren't produced under the Hays code in Hollywood, they have a very visceral and real showcase of stuff like gun and sexual violence, drug use, etc.

Seeing Kurosawa's really masterful control of rhythm, mood and narrative working around source material like this is a delight, without even accounting for the italian neorrealism influence, where none of the criminal protagonists are just nihilistic bad men. All of them are so humanized it even makes me emotional when one of them dies or is caught. Absolutely phenomenal.

His other films in other genres are also fantastic, but the crime/noir types might be more of your liking. *Seven Samurai*'s length clocks at almost 3 and a half hours, but I had never ever gotten bored or unattentive watching it, it's so tightly built up. *Rashomon* and *Ikiru* are also fantastic, in their own specific ways. *Throne of Blood* and *Dodeskaden* I admit not being much into. *Yojimbo*, *Sanjuro*, *The Hidden Fortress*, *Ran* and *Dreams* are very good but not his best.

Anyway, his crime/noir films are my favorites.

In Akira Kurosawa's Dreams there is the segment titled The Tunnel. I will not spoil it, but only to say that even after I first viewed it years ago, it has stayed with me. It's powerful and haunting, and yes, heartbreaking.

The segment was inspired by Akira's trusted friend Ishiro Honda, who was a veteran and experienced recurring nightmares of his lost comrades from the war. He was an advisor regarding military matters, such as the holding of one's rifle when marching, etc. IMDB and other sources have incorrectly written that Ishiro directed the segment, he did not.
It's perfect for an introduction to Kurosawa. Fun story, plenty of comic relief, good action sequences, satisfying ending. And it still has plenty of that classic Kurosawa cinematography to enjoy.

I don't mean to sound like some sort of elitist gatekeeper, but honestly I don't think Akira Kurosawa is that accesible to the genera casual audiences, the people who only watch films for entertainment without consideration of an artistic value. Of course, he has made many films that are very entertaining, but most people are not going to go through the trouble of watching a foreign-language subtitled film, especially when most of them are in black and white. No knock against your friends, but it's probably just outside of their interests. Now there are many people who are more interested in films wihtout being full-on cinephiles, and in that case Akira Kurosawa is a lot more accessible than his contemporaries like Ozu or Bergman. 

If I had to say what his most accessible film is, I would reccomend Yojimbo, but if you think that wouldn't work, I would actually give a somewhat less common reccomendation. A lot of people would obviusly rather watch a color iflm than black and white. Now looking at Kurosawa's color films, Dodes'kaden and Dreams are a little too surrrealistic, Dersu Uzala and Kagemusha are rather slow-paced and can't currently be watched in the *best* quality, so... that leaves Ran. Now Ran is also a pretty slow-paced film, and it might not have the broadest appeal possible. But it is an adaptation of Shakespeare, which is pretty entrenched in popular culture. And the visuals are so striking, that any person would be able to recognize their beauty. So maybe try Ran.
